newsitem.title: THAILAND: Activists to build on ASEAN hestitation on Burma.
newsitem.headline: Activists to build on ASEAN hestitation on Burma.

text.p: Human rights activists said on Wednesday they hoped to capitalise on the apparent hesitation among some Southeast Asian nations for the quick acceptance of Burma into a major regional grouping.

They said the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) appeared to be wavering on its "constructive engagement" approach to Burma given the military regime's poor human rights record and its refusal to negotiate with pro-democracy groups.

Organisers"Alternative ASEAN" meeting of about 80 activists, Burmese exiles and politicians from more than a dozen countries vowed on Wednesday to lobby ASEAN governments to oppose Burma's speedy admission to the grouping.
ASEAN groups Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei and Vietnam. Membership in the forum gives governments access to economic integration and legitimacy.

Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) has applied for ASEAN membership. Rangoon has already been granted observer status, but wants to become a full member at the next formal meeting in July.

"I think there will be a big difference when it is the Asians themselves talking to our governments," said Evelyn Balais-Serrano, an organiser of the "Alternative ASEAN" conference and a consultant to the Asian Forum for Human Rights and Development.

"Before it was the U.S. and European communities urging Asian countries to stop human rights violations...which ASEAN governments thought was foreign intervention," she said. "But this time it will be Asians asking our own governments to take a position with regard to SLORC."

ASEAN has a policy of "constructive engagement" with Burma aimed at keeping the country from becoming isolated and trying to spark reform from within. The policy came under question earlier this month when Philippine President Fidel Ramos said ASEAN leaders might review it.

His comments followed a fresh SLORC crackdown on pro-democracy activists. The government arrested 573 members or supporters of Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) to prevent a party meeting in late September.
The SLORC recently detained and released NLD deputy president Kyi Maung, a key adviser to Suu Kyi.

Thai Foreign Minister Amnuay Viravan was quoted on Wednesday as saying Burma should bring in democracy before it becomes a full ASEAN member. He also said Thailand thinks Burma needs "some time" to prepare for admission as a full member.
Western nations oppose allowing Burma into ASEAN because of the SLORC's human rights record and its refusal to hold talks with Nobel Peace laureate Suu Kyi.

"Definitely, constructive engagement has been a failure in terms of improving the situation in Burma," said Debbie Stothard, coordinator of the Burma Solidarity Group Malaysia and co-organiser of the Alternative ASEAN meeting.

"Now it is up to ASEAN to redefine what is constructive engagement," she said. "ASEAN at the moment is stuck in a deadlock as far as SLORC membership is concerned... The question is will our countries have the courage to redefine their position with the SLORC?"
